newsitem.title: UK: Archbishop Carey on delicate visit to Pope.
newsitem.headline: Archbishop Carey on delicate visit to Pope.

text.p: The Archbishop of Canterbury makes his first official visit to Pope John Paul on Tuesday, keeping alive a difficult Anglican-Catholic dialogue despite formidable differences on issues such as women priests and papal authority.

Archbishop George Carey's three-day visit is expected to be much more low key than a controversial unofficial meeting with the Polish Pontiff in 1992, which was clouded by a row over his direct challenge of the Catholic Church's ban on contraceptives.
Before the 1992 visit, Carey, who became spiritual leader of the world's 70 million Anglican communion in 1990, made a series of statements that had irked the Vatican.
Four years on, the dust from the bust up over Anglican women's ordination -- and the hundreds of Anglican priests who have converted to Rome because of it -- seems to have settled.

"Both sides have stood their ground on women priests and other issues so I don't expect any fireworks," said a Vatican source in Rome. "But the visit is important as a symbol that the dialogue is continuing despite difficulties."

Carey and the conservative, ailing 76-year-old Pope, now in the 19th year of his pontificate, are expected to stress their commitment to eventual unity between the Churches which split in 1534 when King Henry VIII refused to accept Papal authority.
Carey will hold two rounds of private talks during his visit to the centre of Christianity.
Significantly, they will worship together in the same Rome church from where St Augustine, the first archbishop of Canterbury, set off for England 1,400 years ago this year.

A host of difficulties -- some theological minutiae and others burning current issues -- remain despite the advances made in a 30-year Anglican-Catholic theological dialogue which has produced two major reports.

"Matters like the validity of Anglican orders or women priests and Anglican concerns about Marian dogmas or even the issue of infallibility itself have to be dealt with within the context of the dialogue," said Reverend Richard Marsh, Carey's Secretary for Ecumenical Affairs.

"I hope we will have a chance for taking stock; for an overview of the last 30 years which have brought so many advances. I hope that out of it will come a commitment to move forward and for some sort of idea of how that moving forward will take place," Marsh told BBC Radio 4's Sunday Programme.

Since the Church of England, mother Church of the Anglican Communion, began ordaining women in 1994, a handful of bishops, more than 300 clergy and thousands of lay members have converted to Catholicism.

A few homesick converts have even returned back to Anglicanism. But both sides have been at pains not to appear triumphalistic over conversions or returns to the fold, even when they involve well-known people.
Women priests is the most formidable obstacle to unity.

In 1995 the Vatican said the Catholic ban on female ordination was a definitive, infallible and unquestionable part of Church doctrine. The ruling would make it difficult if not impossible for a future Pope to change the ruling for some time.

The Catholic Church says it does not have the authority to allow women to become priests because Christ, in a free and sovereign way, chose only men as his apostles and was therefore reflecting "divine will".
Supporters of a female Catholic priesthood say Christ was only acting according to the customs of his times.
Papal primacy -- recognition of the Pope's supreme authority over any unified Christian church -- has been one of the most thorny issues facing theologians in ecumenical dialogue.

In a move with potentially historic consequences, the Pope said in a 1995 encyclical that for the sake of unity he was willing to seek an accommodation with other Christian denominations on the future role of the papacy.
But he made clear he would not accept a symbolic papacy without teeth and that Rome would have to hold the primary place among Christians because St Peter, the first Pope, died there.
